title: A Visitor for the Well
premise: Tamsin Thornbury, an urban explorer haunted by ten years of unexplained noises beneath the city, is hired to document a construction site where the crew has unearthed a door sealed from the inside. The tunnels predate every survey, and they remember her: her missing father descended in 1974 as part of a crew that took something from the well at their heart — a name, spoken aloud, that kept the frost at bay. As winter deepens, the cold begins writing patterns on skin, glass, and memory, claiming the crew one by one. Tamsin must descend, recover what was taken, and speak it back into the well before the final pattern completes — but returning it means surrendering the version of herself she built to survive, and she does so, sealing the door behind her from the inside.
about_author: Bram Lockridge is the pen name of a former municipal surveyor who spent two decades mapping infrastructure no one wanted documented. Their fiction draws on the quiet dread of places that appear on no official record.

chapters.title: The Survey That Isn't
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She maps a storm tunnel that contradicts every city record, noting the familiar rhythmic knocking she's heard for a decade. She tells herself it's water pressure. Emotional beat: disciplined denial cracking at the edges.

chapters.title: Break Ground
chapters.summary: Tamsin is contracted to document the Harrow Street excavation. The crew hits a void; foreman Dev Okafor shows her a stone door, its iron ring fused, sealed from within. Tamsin recognizes the masonry style from her own unauthorized maps. Beat: dread of recognition.

chapters.title: Sealed From the Inside
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She photographs the door and finds, in the mortar, a scratched date: 1974 — the year her father vanished. At night she dreams of frost ferns growing across a window that isn't there. Beat: the past reaching forward.

chapters.title: The Knocking Answers
chapters.summary: Alternating POV with Dev. Overnight, the knocking Tamsin knows so well begins inside the sealed chamber — three knocks, pause, three. Dev dismisses it; Tamsin cannot. Beat: denial becomes untenable.

chapters.title: What Dad Left in the Boot
chapters.summary: Tamsin searches her mother's storage unit and finds her father's field kit: a lantern, a notebook with pages torn out, and a brass token stamped with a spiral. A note reads 'If it knocks, don't answer twice.' Beat: inheritance of guilt.

chapters.title: First Frost
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. An unseasonal cold settles over the site. Worker Priya Raman finds frost ferns blooming on the inside of her truck windows — while parked indoors. Beat: the rules of reality bending.

chapters.title: The Notebook's Missing Pages
chapters.summary: Tamsin matches the torn stubs in her father's notebook to archive microfilm: a 1974 municipal project, six names, all listed as relocated. One name is her father's. Another belongs to the site's elderly landowner, Edith Vane. Beat: the conspiracy narrows.

chapters.title: Edith Vane Remembers Wrong
chapters.summary: Tamsin interviews Edith, who recounts 1974 vividly but places herself elsewhere during the collapse — until Tamsin mentions the spiral token and Edith's hands begin tracing frost patterns on the tablecloth without her noticing. Beat: memory as unreliable shelter.

chapters.title: Priya Stops Sleeping
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Priya reports hearing her own voice calling from below ground. Frost appears on her skin in feathering lines that fade by morning but leave her forgetting small things — her address, then her sister's face. Beat: the cost made personal.

chapters.title: The Well Beneath
chapters.summary: Tamsin descends through a crawlway from her own mapped tunnels and reaches the far side of the sealed door. Through a fissure she sees a dry stone well, its rim carved with spirals, and something pale turning slowly at its bottom. Beat: awe curdling into horror.

chapters.title: Six Names
chapters.summary: Tamsin confronts Edith with the full list. Edith breaks: in 1974 the crew found the well and heard a voice offering to 'hold the winter off' if they gave it a name to keep. They gave it her brother's. He walked down willingly. The door was sealed behind him. Beat: confession and inherited sin.

chapters.title: The Pattern Completes
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Priya is found standing at the excavation edge at 3 a.m., frost covering half her body in a finished design. She survives but no longer remembers Tamsin, or the site, or why she came. Beat: escalation — the well is collecting.

chapters.title: It Knows My Name
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The knocking changes rhythm — it spells her childhood nickname in code her father taught her. The well doesn't want just any name now; it wants hers, or his. Beat: hunted by something patient.

chapters.title: What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Tamsin deciphers her father's remaining notes: they didn't give the well a person — they gave it his true name, the one he'd hidden even from family, and the well held his identity as collateral. Without it returned, the frost collects substitutes. Beat: understanding the price.

chapters.title: The Crew Walks Out
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Two workers quit mid-shift, leaving their tools standing upright in frozen mud. Dev stays — his brother works nights downtown, and the cold front is spreading along the old tunnel lines toward the city. Beat: reluctant commitment.

chapters.title: Opening the Door
chapters.summary: Tamsin, Dev, and Edith use the brass token as a key in the door's spiral lock. It opens inward, exhaling air that smells of snow on stone. Edith refuses to enter; she says the well already has enough of her. Beat: threshold crossed.

chapters.title: The Long Descent
chapters.summary: Tamsin and Dev descend the shaft. Frost ferns grow under their boots with each step, mapping their progress like a ledger. Tamsin hears her father's voice reciting the nickname-code, leading her deeper. Beat: surrender to the pull.

chapters.title: The Man at the Bottom
chapters.summary: At the well's base they find her father — not decayed, not aged, but hollowed, repeating fragments of a life that no longer cohere. He doesn't recognize her. The pale thing turning in the well wears his missing years like frost wears breath. Beat: grief without reunion.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Tamsin speaks her father's true name back into the well. The frost patterns reverse; the pale thing stills. But the well demands balance — a name given must be replaced by a name surrendered. Her father collapses into ordinary mortality and dies gently, finally free. Beat: costly victory.

chapters.title: The Final Pattern
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. The cold retreats up the shaft, but the well turns its attention to Tamsin, who feels her own memories beginning to feather at the edges. She realizes returning the name means giving the well hers. Dev begs her to run. Beat: the choice crystallized.

chapters.title: A Visitor for the Well
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She gives the well her name willingly — not taken, offered — which the terms allow. She walks down as her father once did, leaving Dev the notebook, now complete. The frost stops. The knocking ends. Beat: sacrifice as authorship of self.

chapters.title: Sealed From the Inside
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Dev's POV. Months later, the site is poured over with concrete. Dev publishes nothing, keeps the token, and visits Edith, who has begun remembering everything again — including a daughter-shaped absence she can't name. On the last page of the notebook, new handwriting: 'Thank you.' Beat: mourning, and terrible peace.
